title: Finding the First Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix: Advanced Cases
sections:
[MATH: [1|0; 2|0; 0|0]]
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that [MATH: A=U \Sigma V^T] is a singular value decomposition of [MATH: A,] find a [MATH: 3\times 3] matrix that could be the matrix [MATH: U.]

Recall that if [MATH: A=U \Sigma V^T] is a singular value decomposition of a [MATH: 3 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A,] then

- [MATH: \Sigma] is a [MATH: 3 \times 2] matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,
- [MATH: U] is an orthogonal [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix,
- [MATH: V] is an orthogonal [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix.

From the matrix [MATH: \Sigma,] we deduce that [MATH: \sigma_1=\sqrt5] and [MATH: \sigma_2=0.]
Also, the columns [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] of [MATH: V] give us the right singular vectors of [MATH: A.]

Therefore, we can compute the [MATH: 1]st column of [MATH: U] as follows:

[MATH: u_{1}|= (1)/(σ_{1})Av_{1}; = (1)/(sqrt(5))[1|0; 2|0; 0|0][1; 0]; = (1)/(sqrt(5))[1; 2; 0]; = [(1)/(sqrt(5)); (2)/(sqrt(5)); 0]]

Since the second singular value is [MATH: \sigma_2=0], and we do not have a third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of [MATH: U.] But we know that [MATH: U] must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors

[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; x_{3}]]

such that [MATH: \mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0] and [MATH: \|\mathbf{u}\|=1.]

Solving [MATH: \mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0,] which is equivalent to
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} x_1 + \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} x_2 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_1 + 2x_2 = 0,]
we get the general solution

[MATH: [− 2x_{2}; x_{2}; x_{3}]]

where [MATH: x_2] and [MATH: x_3] are free variables. Notice that the two linearly independent solutions are mutually orthogonal. Normalizing these vectors, we get

[MATH: [− (2)/(sqrt(5)); (1)/(sqrt(5)); 0]]

Finally, we construct the matrix [MATH: U \mathbin{:}]

[MATH: [(1)/(sqrt(5))|− (2)/(sqrt(5))|0; (2)/(sqrt(5))|(1)/(sqrt(5))|0; 0|0|1]]

title: Finding the First Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix: Cases Requiring Orthogonalization
sections:
[MATH: [sqrt(2)|0; 1|0; − 1|0]]
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that [MATH: A=U \Sigma V^T] is a singular value decomposition of [MATH: A,] find a [MATH: 3\times 3] matrix that could be the matrix [MATH: U.]

Recall that if [MATH: A=U \Sigma V^T] is a singular value decomposition of a [MATH: 3 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A,] then

- [MATH: \Sigma] is a [MATH: 3 \times 2] matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,
- [MATH: U] is an orthogonal [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix,
- [MATH: V] is an orthogonal [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix.

From the matrix [MATH: \Sigma,] we deduce that [MATH: \sigma_1=2] and [MATH: \sigma_2=0.]
Also, the columns [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] of [MATH: V] give us the right singular vectors of [MATH: A.]

Therefore, we can compute the [MATH: 1]st column of [MATH: U] as follows:

[MATH: u_{1}|= (1)/(σ_{1})Av_{1}; = (1)/(2)[sqrt(2)|0; 1|0; − 1|0][1; 0]; = (1)/(2)[sqrt(2); 1; − 1]; = [(sqrt(2))/(2); (1)/(2); − (1)/(2)]]

Since the second singular value is [MATH: \sigma_2=0], and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of [MATH: U.] But we know that [MATH: U] must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors

[MATH: [u_{1}; u_{2}; u_{3}]]

such that [MATH: \mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0] and [MATH: \|\mathbf{u}\|=1.]

Solving [MATH: \mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0,] which is equivalent to
[MATH: \dfrac{\sqrt2}{2} x_1 + \dfrac{1}{2} x_2- \dfrac{1}{2} x_3 = 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\sqrt2x_1 + x_2-x_3 = 0,]
we get the general solution

[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; sqrt(2)x_{1} + x_{2}]]

where [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions [MATH: \mathbf{b}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}_2] are not mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let

[MATH: [1; 0; sqrt(2)]]

Then,

[MATH: c_{2}|= b_{2} − (b_{2} ⋅ c_{1})/(c_{1} ⋅ c_{1})c_{1}; = [0; 1; 1] − (sqrt(2))/(3)[1; 0; sqrt(2)]; = (1)/(3)[− sqrt(2); 3; 1].]

Finally, normalizing the orthogonal vectors [MATH: \mathbf{c}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{c}_2,] we obtain the second and third columns of [MATH: U{:}]

[MATH: [(1)/(sqrt(3)); 0; (sqrt(2))/(sqrt(3))]]

So, the matrix [MATH: U] could be the following:

[MATH: [(sqrt(2))/(2)|(1)/(sqrt(3))|− (sqrt(2))/(2sqrt(3)); (1)/(2)|0|(3)/(2sqrt(3)); − (1)/(2)|(sqrt(2))/(sqrt(3))|(1)/(2sqrt(3))]]
